rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The retention pattern will identify critical pairs and guide window trimming and slope or temperature changes.

Only the first pair limits the score, while the last peak already elutes within 10 minutes. Raising temperature with the gradient unchanged tests whether thermal selectivity resolves that pair while preserving the time advantage.

Injection 2 reached the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to test whether full resolution can be maintained with earlier elution, watching the first pair closely.

Narrowing the gradient window slightly reduces steepness, targeting recovery of the first pair to R ≥ 1.5 while retaining faster elution than injection 2. The final organic fraction remains comfortably above the estimated last-peak elution fraction.

Shift the gradient window upward while keeping its slope unchanged to reduce elution times. This tests whether the first pair retains full resolution with less initial retention; injection 4 remains the faster confirmed maximum-score method.

Test the low-temperature selectivity regime with a steeper gradient to offset increased retention. This explores whether a different elution-order pattern can resolve the first pair in a shorter run, while retaining injection 4 as the confirmed maximum-score benchmark.

Raise temperature one step from injection 6 to separate the late three-peak cluster while testing whether the first pair remains resolved. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates the temperature effect in this alternative selectivity regime.

At 30 C the late cluster is separating but still limits resolution; another temperature step should improve it. Raising the starting organic fraction tests whether shifting the elution window can preserve early-pair selectivity and shorten the run.

Lengthen injection 8's gradient by one step to test whether the first pair reaches full resolution while the late pairs remain separated. This isolates the slope response at 35 C and should keep the last peak within 10 minutes.

Return to the confirmed high-temperature selectivity and trim the gradient endpoint, giving a slope close to injection 4 with a shorter programmed gradient. The first pair should remain fully resolved, and the last peak is expected to elute inside the gradient near 7 minutes.

This slightly steeper, shorter gradient tests the first pair near its full-resolution boundary. The last peak may move into the final hold, so this run will establish whether the lower endpoint still permits a faster maximum-score separation.

Test whether a shallower gradient compensates for the first-pair resolution lost at the higher starting organic fraction in injection 5. This explores an alternative maximum-score window while retaining injection 11 as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test a higher starting fraction with a shallower slope to determine whether early-pair resolution can be recovered after further window trimming. The endpoint remains above the observed high-temperature elution window, limiting the risk of a long final hold.

Explore a shorter low-temperature method with a higher starting fraction, testing whether the changed solvent window separates the late cluster seen in injection 6. Low temperature may preserve early-pair selectivity, while the high endpoint ensures strong elution.

The low-temperature late cluster needs both improved thermal selectivity and a shallower gradient. This method tests whether those changes resolve the cluster while retaining the early-pair separation, with injection 11 preserved as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Raise temperature one step with injection 15's gradient unchanged to improve the remaining late-pair resolution and shorten retention. The early pair has some resolution margin, so this tests whether both critical regions can be fully resolved simultaneously.

Return to the high-temperature optimum and test a slope between the fully resolved injection 11 and slightly under-resolved injection 3. This probes whether the last peak can elute earlier than 6.97 minutes while keeping the first pair at R ≥ 1.5.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 12 at the same starting fraction, targeting its small first-pair resolution margin. This refines the alternative high-temperature window near the full-resolution boundary while retaining injection 11 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

The fastest confirmed method has little resolution margin, so test a shallower gradient for a more robust maximum-score alternative. This should strengthen the first pair while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes; monitor the third–fourth pair, whose resolution decreases with shallower slopes.

Trim injection 2's endpoint while preserving its successful gradient slope, targeting the same full resolution with a shorter programmed gradient. The last peak should still elute before the gradient ends, providing more resolution margin than injection 11.

Raise the endpoint one grid step from injection 11 to accelerate the last peak and eliminate its final-hold delay. This tests the faster boundary of the best short-gradient method, though the first pair's narrow resolution margin may be lost.

Back off the gradient steepness to restore a comfortable first-pair resolution margin while retaining a six-minute programmed gradient. This tests whether the lower endpoint still elutes the last compound within 10 minutes despite a longer final hold.

Test a slope near injection 19's balance between the two critical early pairs, with a trimmed endpoint that should still keep all peaks inside the gradient. This targets a maximum-score method with roughly R = 2 resolution margins, while injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved option.

Combine the higher starting fraction with a shallower gradient to improve first-pair resolution while preserving the larger third–fourth-pair separation seen at phi0 = 0.10. This tests a trimmed-window maximum-score alternative with more resolution margin than the fastest confirmed method, injection 11.

Raise injection 24's endpoint to shorten retention, using a slope slightly shallower than the fully resolved injection 18 to preserve first-pair resolution. This targets another maximum-score method near 7.3 minutes; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method at 6.97 minutes.
